quote: Das Lagrange Problem $ax^n + bx^{n-1}y + \cdots = 2^m$ durch ganze Zahlen zu lösen.
english: To solve the Lagrange problem ax^n + bx^{n-1}y + ... = 2^m in integers.
topic: A list of research ideas in invariant theory: groups of operations arising from irrational covariants, covariants defined by vanishing transvectants of binary forms of degree 7 and 10, a generalisation of Gordan's problem on sextic forms, vanishing transvectants of a form with its transform, re-proving a theorem of the dissertation by infinitesimal transformations, and a Lagrange problem on solving a binary form equal to a power of 2 in integers.

triage.modern_statement: Take a binary form F(x,y) = a x^n + b x^{n-1} y + ... + k y^n with integer coefficients. The task is to find all integers x, y, m ≥ 0 such that F(x,y) = 2^m. In modern terms this is a Thue–Mahler equation, F(x,y) = c·p1^z1···ps^zs, here with the single prime p = 2. The usual non-degeneracy assumptions are n ≥ 3, F having at least three pairwise non-proportional linear factors over the complex numbers, and gcd(x,y) = 1 (or gcd(x,y,2) = 1). Under these assumptions the questions are whether there are finitely many solutions and how to find all of them. Without such conditions the problem can be degenerate: for example, F = x^n has infinitely many solutions x = 2^k.
triage.answered_by: Finiteness was proved by Kurt Mahler in 1933, extending Thue's 1909 result for F(x,y) = m with m fixed. Coates (Acta Arith. 15, 1969, and a sequel) made the result effective using Baker's method. Evertse (Crelle 1989 and Inventiones) gave bounds on the number of solutions. Practical algorithms came from Tzanakis–de Weger (c. 1992), from Hambrook's implementation, and from Gherga–Siksek, 'Efficient resolution of Thue–Mahler equations' (arXiv 2022; Algebra & Number Theory 19(4), 2025).

evidence.claim: Thue proved F(p,q) = m has finitely many integer solutions; Mahler extended this to Thue–Mahler equations in 1933. Both original proofs were ineffective. Baker gave the first effective proof for Thue's theorem, and Coates did so for Mahler's theorem.
Coates, 'An effective p-adic analogue of a theorem of Thue', Acta Arith. 15 (1969), 275–305.
The Thue–Mahler equation |F(x,y)| = m p1^z1···pt^zt, and Mahler's 1933 finiteness result, as stated in Evertse's Crelle 1989 paper.
Encyclopedia of Mathematics entry on the Thue–Mahler equation and its S-unit generalisation.
Gherga and Siksek give an efficient algorithm for resolving Thue–Mahler equations F(X,Y) = a·p1^z1···pv^zv. It improves on earlier algorithms such as Tzanakis–de Weger's.
The Gherga–Siksek paper was published in Algebra & Number Theory, Vol. 19 (2025), No. 4.
Survey of Mahler's work on Thue–Mahler equations and later developments, including effective finiteness results and counts of solutions.

triage.why: The note is clearly a binary form set equal to a power of a prime, which is a special case of the Thue–Mahler equation. For non-degenerate forms of degree at least 3, Mahler (1933) proved there are only finitely many solutions. Coates (1969–70) made this effective via Baker's method. Today there are working algorithms (Tzanakis–de Weger; Gherga–Siksek 2022/2025), so the problem is solved in general. Research is still active on efficiency, solution counts and applications. The note is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem. I found no source linking this note to a specific 'Lagrange problem', so that attribution, and exactly which degenerate cases Hilbert meant to allow, remain unconfirmed. This is why confidence is medium, not high.
